title: Mint condition

clues.t: I was born on Christmas Day, so tiny I could reportedly fit inside a quart pot.
I secretly spent decades dabbling in alchemy.
In middle age I became a coin cop, hunting counterfeiters through London's taverns.
I split white light with a prism and showed it was all the colours in disguise.
I had a years-long spat with a German over who invented calculus first.
Legend says a falling apple got me thinking about gravity.

pearl: Physicist, alchemist, Master of the Royal Mint: the original side-hustler. Bonus: the apple tree at his family home, Woolsthorpe Manor, is still standing.

title: Say it three times fast

clues.t: Legend says my first batch tasted so foul it was dumped in a cellar and forgotten.
Years later someone tasted it again and, plot twist, it was delicious.
There are fermented anchovies in me. Vegetarians, check the label.
Two chemists created me in the 1830s and their names are still on my bottle.
I'm a must in a Bloody Mary and a Caesar dressing.
I'm named after an English county, and nobody can pronounce me. Try 'Wuss-ter-sher'.

pearl: Lea & Perrins started selling it in 1837 and still makes it in Worcester. The tongue-twister is half the fun.

title: Nature's group project

clues.t: Under UV light I glow a ghostly blue-green.
I don't have a stomach. My food goes straight to the intestine.
The males pack a venomous spur on each back ankle.
British scientists first thought I was a hoax, stitched together by a prankster.
I'm a mammal that lays eggs, and I hunt with my eyes shut by sensing electricity.
Beaver tail, webbed feet, duck's bill. Australia's weirdest local.

pearl: Platypus mums have no nipples; milk seeps out through patches of skin. The plural is 'platypuses', not 'platypi'.

title: Iron lady

clues.t: I grow up to 15 cm taller in summer.
I get a fresh coat of paint about every seven years, roughly 60 tonnes of it.
I was only supposed to stand for 20 years. Being handy as a radio mast saved me.
My designer kept a private apartment near my top for entertaining guests.
I was the tallest structure humans had ever built until 1930.
I'm made of wrought iron, built for the 1889 World's Fair in Paris.

pearl: Many Parisian artists signed a petition calling it a monstrosity. Now it's the city's most famous selfie backdrop.

title: Cool customer

clues.t: There's an app here so locals can check they aren't dating a cousin.
My last McDonald's burger was bought in 2009 and is still on display, barely decayed.
I have no standing army.
Parents often leave babies napping outside in prams, even in winter.
My parliament, the Althing, dates back to 930.
Volcanoes, glaciers, geysers and a capital called Reykjavík.

pearl: Surnames are mostly 'son of' or 'daughter of', so the phone book is sorted by first name. Very cosy.

title: Mind the gap

clues.t: My earliest version was called the 'clasp locker'.
A Swedish-American engineer made me actually work in 1913.
My famous name came from a rubber company selling galoshes in the 1920s.
One Japanese company, YKK, makes around half of all of me worldwide.
I have two rows of teeth and a slider, but I don't bite. Mostly.
You do me up on jeans, jackets and bags. Check your fly.

pearl: YKK stands for Yoshida Kōgyō Kabushiki-gaisha. Look at your nearest zip; it's probably theirs.

title: Who you gonna...?

clues.t: My famous car started life as a 1959 Cadillac built as an ambulance-hearse combo.
A real New York fire station, Hook & Ladder 8, plays my headquarters.
My villain takes the form of a giant marshmallow man.
I hit cinemas in 1984 and spawned a theme song everyone shouts along to.
Four scientists in jumpsuits wear unlicensed nuclear accelerators on their backs.
Who you gonna call?

pearl: The car's name is Ecto-1. Tip from the film: don't cross the streams.

title: Spooky season's founding mother

clues.t: After I died, my drowned husband's heart was found in my desk, wrapped in a page of his poem.
My mother was a famous early champion of women's rights.
I eloped at 16 with a poet.
In a summer with no sun, Lord Byron challenged friends to write a ghost story. My story beat them all.
My novel, first published anonymously in 1818, is subtitled 'The Modern Prometheus'.
I wrote Frankenstein. And no, the monster isn't called Frankenstein.

pearl: She began it at 18, which makes her the godmother of science fiction. Bonus: 1816's 'year without a summer' was caused by a volcano in Indonesia.
